Q: How to loop a function and save the outputs of each run as independent objects? A:

Use Map and assign the result to list L and then L$mpg etc can get individual components. Alternately use list2env to place the components of L into the global environment. Normally using a list is preferable to having loose objects in the global environment.

# 1
library(dplyr)
 
calculate_summary <- function(var) {
  mtcars %>% 
    dplyr::group_by(cyl, vs) %>% 
    dplyr::summarise(
      N = length(.data[[var]]),
      mean = mean(.data[[var]]),
      sd   = sd(.data[[var]]),
      se   = sd / sqrt(N),
      .groups = "drop")
}
 
L <- Map(calculate_summary, c("mpg", "qsec"))
L$mpg
## # A tibble: 5 × 6
##     cyl    vs     N  mean     sd     se
##   <dbl> <dbl> <int> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
## 1     4     0     1  26   NA     NA    
## 2     4     1    10  26.7  4.75   1.50 
## 3     6     0     3  20.6  0.751  0.433
## 4     6     1     4  19.1  1.63   0.816
## 5     8     0    14  15.1  2.56   0.684

or


# 2
list2env(L, globalenv())
<environment: R_GlobalEnv>

mpg
## # A tibble: 5 × 6
##     cyl    vs     N  mean     sd     se
##   <dbl> <dbl> <int> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
## 1     4     0     1  26   NA     NA    
## 2     4     1    10  26.7  4.75   1.50 
## 3     6     0     3  20.6  0.751  0.433
## 4     6     1     4  19.1  1.63   0.816
## 5     8     0    14  15.1  2.56   0.684

Another approach is to create a single data frame and then filter it:

# 3
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)

DF <- map_dfr(set_names(c("mpg", "qsec")), calculate_summary, .id = "group")
filter(DF, group == "mpg")
## # A tibble: 5 × 7
##   group   cyl    vs     N  mean     sd     se
##   <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <int> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
## 1 mpg       4     0     1  26   NA     NA    
## 2 mpg       4     1    10  26.7  4.75   1.50 
## 3 mpg       6     0     3  20.6  0.751  0.433
## 4 mpg       6     1     4  19.1  1.63   0.816
## 5 mpg       8     0    14  15.1  2.56   0.684

If the last approach is of interest note that the dlookr package works with group_by eliminating calculate_summary.

# 4
library(dlookr)
library(dplyr)

DF2 <- mtcars %>%
  group_by(cyl, vs) %>%
  describe(mpg, qsec, statistics = c("mean", "sd", "se_mean"))

filter(DF2, described_variables == "mpg")
## # A tibble: 5 × 8
##   described_variables   cyl    vs     n    na  mean     sd se_mean
##   <chr>               <dbl> <dbl> <int> <int> <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>
## 1 mpg                     4     0     1     0  26   NA      NA    
## 2 mpg                     4     1    10     0  26.7  4.75    1.50 
## 3 mpg                     6     0     3     0  20.6  0.751   0.433
## 4 mpg                     6     1     4     0  19.1  1.63    0.816
## 5 mpg                     8     0    14     0  15.1  2.56    0.684

or to produce a list without calculate_summary add a split at the end:

# 5
library(dlookr)
library(dplyr)

L2 <- mtcars %>% 
  group_by(cyl, vs) %>%
  describe(mpg, qsec, statistics = c("mean", "sd", "se_mean")) %>%
  { split(select(., -described_variables), .$described_variables) }
L2$mpg
## # A tibble: 5 × 7
##     cyl    vs     n    na  mean     sd se_mean
##   <dbl> <dbl> <int> <int> <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>
## 1     4     0     1     0  26   NA      NA    
## 2     4     1    10     0  26.7  4.75    1.50 
## 3     6     0     3     0  20.6  0.751   0.433
## 4     6     1     4     0  19.1  1.63    0.816
## 5     8     0    14     0  15.1  2.56    0.684

Q: How to compute the between-group mean difference? A:

Not sure if this is what you are looking for?

out %>% 
    drop_na() %>% 
    select(-c(ID, Gender, Age, Education)) %>% 
    group_by(tests0) %>% 
    ungroup() %>% 
    pivot_wider(names_from = GROUP, values_from = contains('score'), values_fn = mean) %>% 
    transmute(
        tests0 = tests0,
        diff0 = score0_TRAINING - score0_CONTROL,
        diff7 = score7_TRAINING - score7_CONTROL
    )
# A tibble: 1 x 3
  tests0     diff0  diff7
  <fct>      <dbl>  <dbl>
1 ADAS_CogT0  1.76 -0.878

Q: How to rewrite the same code with across function A:

I thought of a possible workaround (that may or may not help) by using across() "manually", without applying functions one column at a time. The resulting output is a data.frame with list columns that are deeply nested, so unnest() will come in handy. I also used possibly() to address the case when two columns are not present, remember that across() can match any number of columns and t.test() needs x and y arguments.

Code:

library(tidyverse)

data <-
  df %>%
  group_by(tests0, GROUP) %>%
  summarize(
    all = list(across(starts_with("score")) %>%
      {
        tibble(
          ttest   = data.frame(possibly(~ reduce(., ~ t.test(.x, .y, paired = TRUE))[c("estimate", 'p.value')], NA)(.)),
          means   = data.frame(map(., ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% set_names(., str_replace(names(.), "\\D+", "mean"))),
          stderrs = data.frame(map(., ~ sd(.x, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% set_names(., str_replace(names(.), "\\D+", "stederr")))
        )
      })
  )
#> `summarise()` has grouped output by 'tests0'. You can override using the `.groups` argument.


data %>%
  unnest(all) %>%
  unnest(-c("tests0", "GROUP"))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 8
#> # Groups:   tests0 [1]
#>   tests0     GROUP    estimate p.value mean0 mean7 stederr0 stederr7
#>   <fct>      <fct>       <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 ADAS_CogT0 CONTROL     -1.24 0.00471  12.5  13.5     3.72     4.81
#> 2 ADAS_CogT0 TRAINING     1.40 0.00295  14.0  12.6     4.55     4.15

Q: Time limit exceeded in Strings Rotations of Each Other A:

indexOf searches starting from the start of the String, whilst lastIndexOf starts the search from the end. See here and here. So, if s2.equals(s1.substring(n) + s.substring(0, n)), then, if n is 1, that would mean that indexOf first needs to pass n - 1 characters until it gets to the first character of the match and then process n further characters, totalling n - 1 + n = 2n - 1 characters and in this case lastIndexOf would pass 1 character at the end until it reaches the last character of the match and the continuing n further characters, totalling n + 1 character and since 2n - 1 < n + 1 if we presume n to be a large positive, it could have yielded the difference in performance that resulted being the straw that broke the camel's back.

But this difference is casual, not a relevant algorithmic difference, because n could be s2.length() - 1 in which case indexOf would be the quicker one.

Hence, there is no known performance hits in using lastIndex vs. lastIndexOf in general, but actual measures may be different if the test cases so suggest. So, instead of trying to find the esoteric difference, it makes more sense to try and see why your algorithm is not quick-enough so it depends on the test cases. For example

if(s1.equals(s2))   return true;

checks whether two, potentially huge strings are equal and it is time-consuming. Maybe it's worth checking whether the first character matches before doing the big check, like

if((s1.charAt(0) == s2.charAt(0)) && s1.equals(s2))   return true;
